chapter: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
title: King, Conn, Buescher and Selmer saxophones
summary: Welburn and McRae sort out which horn he played and discuss the popularity of King, Conn and Buescher, and the arrival of Selmer in 1938.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: You were playing a tenor at that time.
Yeah. Tenor and then he put me on clarinet.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
I was playing -- that was a King horn. Remember that big bell that King used to have. That was a King horn.
No, no, not a King. What was that, you'd mentioned a King to me. It wasn't a King.
They were very popular in the (inaudible).
Yeah. Well King was too. Because most of your band instruments were King. Must remember mostly all the schools and colleges bought King instruments.
Well it was popular, it was good. But it wasn't as popular as some of the King horns.
King was most of the big bands, the great big silver bass, and things like that -- was a King horn.
But the Conn was the most thing you'd buy -- dance bands and things. And Conn made a lot of band stuff too. They were very popular.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Until -- I forget the year that Selmer came in. I think Selmer came in in '38 was when it hit this country.
Because '37 when Coleman Hawkins was in Europe, they tell me he was blowing a Selmer horn, we was asking, 'What's that horn that Coleman Hawkins use?' And that was Selmer.
